analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to anyone who wants to buy in, creating a public health insurance option.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let each state open its Medicaid program to residents who aren't already eligible for it, so anyone could buy in and get government-backed health coverage at capped prices, with federal subsidies available to help pay premiums. It would also have raised what Medicaid pays primary care doctors to Medicare levels, given extra federal money to states that expand Medicaid, and required Medicaid to cover abortion services. It was referred to two House committees in August 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, uninsured and underinsured Americans in participating states could buy government-backed Medicaid coverage with premiums capped at 8.5% of family income and ACA-style subsidies applied to those premiums, typically cheaper than private marketplace plans. States that had not yet expanded Medicaid would get the enhanced federal matching rate if they did, and Medicaid patients would benefit from higher primary care payment rates [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Starting January 1, 2022, residents not eligible for Medicaid and not enrolled in other coverage could buy into their state's Medicaid plan, with premiums and cost-sharing capped at ACA levels, as a state option.

Buy-in enrollees could use ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions toward their Medicaid premiums, and the plan would be sold through the ACA exchanges, making coverage meaningfully cheaper than typical marketplace plans.
The bill restores a requirement that Medicaid pay primary care doctors, nurse practitioners, and clinics at Medicare rates, aiming to expand the doctors who accept Medicaid patients.
It requires Medicaid to cover comprehensive reproductive health care, including abortion, and gives every state that expands Medicaid the enhanced federal matching rate regardless of when it expands.

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers would face a low-priced public competitor for individual customers. The federal government would cover 90% of buy-in administrative costs and the higher primary care payment floor; states choosing to participate would bear remaining administrative costs [S3].

drawbacks.text: The buy-in is not free: states may charge premiums up to 8.5% of family income plus cost-sharing capped at ACA levels, though the bill lets enrollees use the same premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions available on the exchanges [S3].

Participation is optional for states, so residents of states that decline would get no new option at all; the bill also permanently raises the federal Medicaid matching rate for late-expanding states and requires all state Medicaid programs to cover abortion services, both of which drew predictable opposition [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real and large: a lower-priced public insurance option for people priced out of private coverage, better primary care payment so doctors actually accept the plan, and guaranteed abortion coverage in Medicaid. The honest costs are that premiums can rise to 8.5% of family income (federal subsidies moderate this), states could opt out and leave residents behind, and insurers and provider groups would fight it hard because it undercuts their pricing power. It died without a fight, so those tradeoffs were never debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and a Health subcommittee in August 2021 and nothing else ever happened to it before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kim Schrier introduced the State Public Option Act on August 6, 2021, with 15 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and shortly after to the Health subcommittee [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers keep the individual market to themselves, and the status quo of expensive exchange coverage and low Medicaid provider pay continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo

for.name: 15 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican support.

against.name: Private health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Public-option proposals of this kind are perennially opposed by insurers, who would lose individual-market customers; no industry lobbying appears in the bill record itself.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans supported it, and with control split between chambers, the bill never advanced beyond referral.

industries.note: A Medicaid-based public option priced below typical marketplace plans would compete directly with private insurers for individual customers. The bill died, so their market position was untouched.

Higher Medicaid primary care payment rates would help primary care providers, but a cheaper public option would pressure provider reimbursement generally. The bill also required Medicaid managed care companies to pass the higher primary care rates through to doctors.
